edbDesc: (often just called the Rayleigh instability). A falling stream of fluid breaks up into smaller packets with the same volume but less surface area by virtue of its surface tension Related to the Rayleigh-Taylor instability.
title: Plateau-Rayleigh instability
description: A thin stream of water from a tap doesn't stay a smooth thread: it wobbles and breaks into a row of drops, because surface tension pulls it into shapes with less surface. Joseph Plateau measured it in 1873 and Lord Rayleigh explained its timing in 1878. Vibrating the jet at the right pitch makes perfectly even drops, the basis of the inkjet printers that mark dates on cans.
effect: a thin stream of liquid breaks itself into a row of equal drops
usedIn: Continuous inkjet printers that print dates on cans and bottles
Making uniform droplets for capsules and beads
strength: A stream breaks into drops spaced about 4.5 stream-widths apart, each roughly twice the stream's width; an inkjet nozzle makes over 60,000 drops a second this way.
pickWhy: Specific named effect with a clear job (making even drops).
